output.query: transient aphasia migraine aura versus transient ischaemic attack clinical features

results.finding: Migraine aura is one of the commonest TIA mimics. Positive symptoms, gradual build-up or spread over minutes, successive involvement of different functions, previous similar attacks and a following headache favour aura; TIA symptoms are usually negative and maximal at onset.
results.source: Nadarajan V, Perry RJ, Johnson J, Werring DJ. Transient ischaemic attacks: mimics and chameleons. Pract Neurol 2014;14:23-31

results.finding: Speech or language disturbance is a typical aura symptom (1.2.1), and aphasia is always regarded as a unilateral symptom. The diagnosis requires at least two attacks and at least three of six aura characteristics.
results.source: Headache Classification Committee of the International Headache Society. ICHD-3. Cephalalgia 2018;38:1-211

output.summary: Gradually evolving symptoms, stereotyped recurrence and a following headache favour migraine aura over TIA; language disturbance is a typical aura symptom under ICHD-3.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Four stereotyped language attacks building over minutes, 15-25 min, fully reversible and followed by migrainous headache: 4 of 6 ICHD-3 C characteristics; no seizure features; red flags are the new language aura and headache on over-anticoagulation
action_criteria.label: Take a structured headache and aura history with neurological examination and red-flag review, applying each ICHD-3 1.2 criterion
action_criteria.rationale: The diagnosis is clinical: the attack count, build-up, duration, laterality, positive symptoms and headache relation separate migraine aura from TIA, and the red-flag review decides whether imaging is needed.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No infarct on DWI and no haemorrhage or microbleeds on SWI; three punctate non-specific subcortical white matter foci, unchanged from the outside study
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI with DWI and susceptibility imaging: a new isolated language aura pattern and headache while over-anticoagulated
action_criteria.rationale: Recommended for red flags: a new isolated aphasic aura (infarct must be excluded) and headache on warfarin with an INR of 3.8 (haemorrhage must be excluded). The outside MRI is re-read against the new study. MRI does not establish migraine.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Sinus rhythm with atrial ectopy at the palpitation triggers; no atrial fibrillation or flutter over 14 days
action_criteria.label: Prolonged ambulatory ECG monitoring (14-30 days) for the palpitations recorded elsewhere as AF
action_criteria.rationale: The AF label rests on a single rhythm strip during palpitations and a 24-hour Holter is too short to exclude paroxysmal AF. A 14-30 day monitor characterises the palpitations. It does not decide anticoagulation: with the attacks recognised as aura her CHA2DS2-VA score is 0 whatever it shows (Van Gelder IC et al., Eur Heart J 2024).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Paracetamol taken regularly potentiates warfarin; NSAIDs and aspirin increase bleeding on warfarin, so an NSAID waits until warfarin has stopped and the INR is normal; a triptan has no interaction
action_criteria.label: Check warfarin against her paracetamol and the candidate acute migraine drugs (NSAIDs, aspirin, triptans) before planning acute treatment
action_criteria.rationale: Required: she is over-anticoagulated (INR 3.8) with mucosal bleeding and treats each headache with paracetamol; the safe acute treatment until warfarin has worn off depends on these interactions.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence on features separating migraine aura from TIA
action_criteria.label: Literature on the clinical features that separate migraine aura from TIA
action_criteria.rationale: Background evidence only; not a clinical step in the pathway.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not continue warfarin or start an antiplatelet for presumed TIA: the attacks have the features of migraine aura (language disturbance building over minutes, previous identical attacks, headache after each) and imaging shows no infarct
Do not give NSAIDs or aspirin for headache while she is still anticoagulated with an above-range INR
required_recommendations: Revise the diagnosis to migraine with typical (language) aura and explain it to the patient and, in writing, to her GP and the referring team, so that the TIA label is removed from her record

Stop warfarin now, without bridging and without a replacement antiplatelet: the attacks are migraine aura, not TIA, and even if paroxysmal AF were later confirmed her CHA2DS2-VA score would be 0 (ESC 2024)

Manage the over-anticoagulation by severity: at INR 3.8 with minor gum and nose bleeding, withholding warfarin is enough; vitamin K is for an INR of 4.5 or more with high bleeding risk, and IV vitamin K 5-10 mg with prothrombin complex concentrate for clinically significant bleeding (Tran HA et al., Med J Aust 2013)

Acute treatment: a triptan (for example sumatriptan 50-100 mg) taken at headache onset rather than during the aura, with an antiemetic if needed; an NSAID such as naproxen 500 mg only after warfarin has stopped and the INR is normal; limit acute medication days to avoid medication overuse
No preventive treatment at about four attacks a year (below the AHS 2021 thresholds); keep a headache diary and reassess if attacks become more frequent or prolonged

If HRT is wanted for menopausal symptoms, migraine with aura is not a contraindication: prefer transdermal oestradiol at the lowest effective dose, with micronised progesterone or a levonorgestrel IUS for endometrial protection, and review if the aura changes (NICE NG23)

avoided_actions.rationale: Head CT adds radiation without adding information here: MRI with susceptibility imaging answers both the infarct and the haemorrhage question in this outpatient setting.
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura and is hazardous on warfarin with an INR of 3.8; there is no suspicion of subarachnoid haemorrhage or meningitis.
MR angiography is not indicated: there is no infarct, no thunderclap headache and no suspicion of dissection or vasculopathy.

Echocardiography (transthoracic or transoesophageal) is not indicated: there is no infarct or embolic event to explain, and the attacks are migraine aura; a TOE also adds procedural risk without diagnostic gain.

accepted: Migraine with aphasic aura (ICHD-3 1.2.1) — misdiagnosed as TIA; warfarin overtreatment causing supratherapeutic INR and bleeding; warfarin should be stopped

differential.key_features: Against: four stereotyped attacks of language disturbance building over about 5 minutes, each followed by migrainous headache; years of brief positive visual phenomena; maternal migraine with aura; no vascular risk factors; MRI shows no infarct. The 'AF' was a single strip during palpitations, and the 24-hour Holter and 14-day monitor show no AF.

differential.diagnosis: Focal seizure with speech arrest or aphasia
differential.key_features: Against: 15-25 minute attacks with gradual build-up and a following migrainous headache; no impaired awareness, automatisms, jerking or post-attack confusion; MRI shows no epileptogenic lesion.
Against: the headache is identical in each attack and follows the aura; no deficit between attacks; MRI shows no haemorrhage or microbleeds on susceptibility imaging.

key_clinical_evidence: The four language attacks meet ICHD-3 1.2.1: speech disturbance building over about 5 minutes, 15-25 minutes long, fully reversible and followed by migrainous headache (4 of 6 characteristics)
The TIA label rested on a single rhythm strip during palpitations reported as AF and on non-specific white matter foci; neither indicates cerebral ischaemia, and the MRI shows no infarct
With the attacks recognised as aura her CHA2DS2-VA score is 0, so warfarin has no indication even if paroxysmal AF were found; the 14-day monitor shows none
Warfarin is causing harm: INR 3.8 with gum bleeding and a prolonged nosebleed
Regular paracetamol and any NSAID or aspirin interact with warfarin; triptans do not

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: It was a single rhythm strip during palpitations; the 24-hour Holter was normal and the 14-day monitor shows no AF. With the attacks recognised as aura her CHA2DS2-VA score is 0, so no anticoagulant is indicated.
red_herrings.data_point: Outside ECG reported as showing 'intermittent AF', and warfarin started for presumed TIA

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Three punctate subcortical foci without infarct or microbleeds are common in migraine and non-specific; they do not indicate TIA.
red_herrings.data_point: Outside MRI reported as showing 'white matter changes'
red_herrings.intended_effect: May appear to support a vascular diagnosis

sequence_constraints.reason: The structured history identifies the red flags that justify imaging.

events.description: Sinus tachycardia 112 bpm with frequent isolated atrial ectopic beats
Sinus rhythm 86 bpm with isolated atrial ectopic beats

findings: No atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter.
Isolated atrial ectopic beats, under 1% of beats; no supraventricular run longer than 3 beats.
Isolated ventricular ectopic beats, under 0.1% of beats; no ventricular tachycardia.
No pause over 2 s; no AV block.
cardiac_monitoring.impression: 1. Sinus rhythm with infrequent atrial ectopy. 2. Both patient-triggered palpitation events correlate with sinus rhythm or sinus tachycardia with atrial ectopic beats. 3. No atrial fibrillation or flutter in 14 days of recording.
cardiac_monitoring.rhythm_summary: Sinus rhythm throughout, rate 52-138 bpm, mean 74 bpm.

findings.result: Four stereotyped attacks in the past 12 months, the first at age 45.

Expressive language disturbance only: word-finding difficulty that builds up over about 5 minutes to halting, effortful speech with preserved comprehension. No visual, sensory, motor or brainstem symptoms during these attacks.
15-25 minutes per attack, with complete recovery of speech each time.
Each attack is followed within about 10 minutes by a severe throbbing left temporal headache with nausea and photophobia lasting 8-12 hours.
For several years, occasional 5-10 minute peripheral visual scintillations ('stars or sparkles'), not reliably followed by headache.
No loss of awareness, automatisms, limb jerking, tongue biting or post-attack confusion reported.
No hypertension, diabetes, smoking or known cardiac disease. One palpitation episode recorded elsewhere on a rhythm strip read as AF; outside 24-hour Holter normal.
Mother had migraine with visual aura.
Paracetamol 1 g as needed for the headaches; warfarin 4 mg daily for 8 months, last INR 3.8.
Fluent speech with normal naming, repetition and comprehension; full visual fields; no motor, sensory, reflex or coordination abnormality. Gingival bleeding on inspection.

Pattern change: present (new language aura after years of brief visual phenomena). Isolated language aura: present. Headache while anticoagulated with an above-range INR: present. Systemic symptoms, neoplasia, deficit outside the aura, sudden onset, onset after 50 (first attack at 45), positional or Valsalva trigger, papilloedema, pregnancy and painful eye: absent.

clinical_assessment.impression: Recurrent stereotyped speech/language aura followed by migrainous headache, meeting ICHD-3 1.2.1 migraine with typical aura (4 attacks; 4 of 6 criterion C characteristics). No seizure features and a low vascular risk profile. Red flags present: new language aura pattern and headache during over-anticoagulation.

scores.ICHD-3 criterion C characteristics met: 4 of 6 (gradual development, 5-60 min duration, unilateral (aphasia counts as unilateral), headache within 60 min)

alternatives: Acute headache treatment while still anticoagulated: a triptan, or paracetamol at occasional doses; NSAIDs only after anticoagulation has ended.
contraindications: NSAIDs and aspirin should not be added to warfarin while the INR is above range and there is mucosal bleeding.
interactions: Warfarin + paracetamol: regular paracetamol of 2 g/day or more for several days raises the INR; occasional single doses have little effect (Hylek EM et al., JAMA 1998;279:657-662; Mahe I et al., Br J Clin Pharmacol 2005;59:371-374). Recheck the INR if paracetamol is taken regularly.
Warfarin + NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac) or aspirin: additive bleeding risk through platelet inhibition and gastric mucosal injury; avoid the combination.
Warfarin + triptans (sumatriptan, rizatriptan, zolmitriptan): no clinically relevant interaction listed.
Warfarin + metoclopramide or prochlorperazine: no clinically relevant interaction listed.
warfarin.proposed: Warfarin 4 mg daily (last INR 3.8) with paracetamol 1 g as needed; acute migraine treatment under consideration
warfarin.summary: Regular paracetamol raises the INR on warfarin and NSAIDs or aspirin add bleeding risk; triptans and common antiemetics do not interact.
warnings: Above-range INR management (Tran HA et al., Med J Aust 2013;198:198-199): INR above range but under 4.5 without clinically significant bleeding, omit or reduce the dose; INR 4.5-10, withhold and consider oral vitamin K 1-2 mg when bleeding risk is high; clinically significant bleeding, IV vitamin K 5-10 mg with prothrombin complex concentrate.
When warfarin is discontinued no taper is needed; the INR returns to normal over several days.

additional_observations: Technique: non-contrast 3 T brain MRI with T1, T2, FLAIR, DWI/ADC and susceptibility-weighted imaging.
Comparison: outside brain MRI 8 months earlier; the white matter foci are unchanged in number and size.
No restricted diffusion. No cortical or subcortical infarct, acute or chronic.
No intracranial haemorrhage, microbleed or superficial siderosis on susceptibility-weighted imaging.
Ventricles and sulci normal for age. No mass, no extra-axial collection.

findings.location: bilateral subcortical frontal and parietal white matter

mri.impression: 1. Three punctate non-specific subcortical white matter hyperintensities in the frontal and parietal lobes, unchanged from the outside study. 2. No acute or chronic infarct, no haemorrhage or microbleeds, no mass.

metadata.condition_name: Migraine with aphasic aura — misdiagnosed as TIA; warfarin overtreatment causing active bleeding
metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: prior TIA misdiagnosis with warfarin treatment causing bleeding complications; recognising TIA misdiagnosis and appropriately stopping anticoagulation; supratherapeutic INR is urgent management priority
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Diagnostic puzzle: deconstructing a prior misdiagnosis, stopping inappropriate anticoagulation, and reframing migraine with aphasic aura

patient.chief_complaint: Recurrent episodes of word difficulty with headache — started on warfarin for 'TIA' 8 months ago; requesting review

family_history: Mother had 'bad headaches with visual aura'; no family history of AF or stroke; no family history of coagulopathy

medications.indication: Presumed TIA (started by the regional hospital team 8 months ago)

social_history.note: Secondary school teacher; non-smoker; 6-8 units alcohol/week; post-menopausal (since age 44); no HRT; no illicit drugs

patient.history_present_illness:
A 46-year-old Australian woman presented to the neurology clinic requesting a second opinion after being started on warfarin 8 months ago for a presumed TIA. She has had four episodes over the past year of transient expressive word-finding difficulty lasting 15-25 minutes, each followed by a severe left temporal throbbing headache with nausea and photophobia lasting 8-12 hours. The treating team at a regional hospital determined that these were 'probable TIA events' and started warfarin after a work-up which included an MRI showing 'white matter changes' and an ECG reportedly showing 'intermittent AF.'

She is now bleeding from her gums and had a prolonged nosebleed last month. Her INR was 3.8 at last check (above therapeutic range). She has no personal history of stroke, no cardiac disease, and was entirely healthy prior to these episodes. On careful history review, she has had occasional brief 'light shows' in her peripheral vision for several years before the main episodes — these were 'like stars or sparkles' lasting 5-10 minutes and dismissed as tiredness.

On review of external records: the 'ECG showing AF' appears to have been a single rhythm strip taken during a palpitation episode; she subsequently had a normal 24-hour Holter. Her mother had 'bad headaches with visual aura' throughout her reproductive years.
